title: Constructors, initializers, and required (object creation)
hook: Construction is how you make an invalid object unrepresentable. Field initializers, constructors, primary constructors, object initializers, and `required` properties are one toolbox — not competing styles.

blocks.text: A **constructor** is a special method that runs when you create an object with `new`. It sets up initial field values after field initializers run. An **object initializer** (`new Type { Prop = value }`) sets properties after the constructor returns. **`required`** (C# 11) is a compiler check that forces callers to set certain properties during creation. **Primary constructors** (C# 12) put parameters directly on the type declaration.

entries.plainDefinition: A method that runs automatically when `new` creates an object. It initializes instance state.
Syntax that sets accessible `set` or `init` properties right after `new`, before the object is used.
A compiler attribute on a property that forces object creation code to set that property, or the build fails.
Constructor parameters declared on the type line itself. They are in scope for the body and field initializers.

blocks.text: Half-built objects are a source of bugs. Validate at the boundary: empty tenant IDs and missing routing keys should throw `ArgumentException` rather than exist as invalid state. `required` plus `init` keeps object initializers honest. Primary constructors reduce boilerplate for types that capture a few inputs.

blocks.title: default(T) bypasses constructors for structs
blocks.body: `default(MyStruct)` zero-initializes all fields and does not run your parameterless constructor. `new MyStruct()` does run it if you wrote one. That split bites configuration structs in arrays and Redis deserialization.

items.title: Field initializers run
items.body: Instance field initializers and property initializers execute first, in declaration order.

items.title: Constructor body runs
items.body: Your constructor code executes. Use `this(...)` to chain to another constructor on the same type.

items.title: Object initializer runs
items.body: If the call site uses `{ Prop = value }`, those assignments happen after the constructor returns.

items.title: Static constructor (once per type)
items.body: Runs before the first use of the type. Keep it tiny — exceptions become `TypeInitializationException` for the process lifetime.

diagram.title: Construction pipeline
diagram.source:
flowchart TD

blocks.title: Construction in C# vs JS/TS
rows: Cannot replace `this` with a different object
JS constructor can return a different object
TS `!` definite assignment is compile-time only, no runtime check
Object literal `{ prop: val }` is the primary pattern
Runs once per type before first use
Module-level code or IIFE — no language equivalent

blocks.title: Object initializers on mutable classes
blocks.body: Setting properties after construction on a mutable class does not create a snapshot. If you need an immutable copy, use `init` properties or records (module 05).

blocks.title: Assuming new() equals default() for structs
blocks.body: If you wrote a parameterless constructor, `new MyStruct()` runs it but `default(MyStruct)` does not. Arrays and `default` always zero-init.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: primary constructors (C# 12) reduce boilerplate but captured parameters are not automatically public — promote to properties when they are part of the contract. Pair `required` with `init` on options classes so RabbitMQ connection strings cannot be forgotten at startup — CS9035 at compile time beats ArgumentNullException at 3 a.m. `SetsRequiredMembers` on factory constructors is an escape hatch for source generators; document why. For structs, `default(T)` zero-inits without running your parameterless constructor — a common bug in pooled struct arrays.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Capture DI inputs on the type
Not every captured param should be public
required string? still allows null value

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying required forbids null. Assuming new MyStruct() equals default(MyStruct) when a ctor exists. Using primary constructor parameters as implicit public API without intent. Not knowing static constructor failure poisons the type.

interviewTakeaways: Primary constructors capture inputs; promote to properties for public API.
required forces initializer assignment — combine with non-nullable types when null is invalid.
default(T) on structs bypasses instance constructors.
60s: Primary ctor for capture. required plus init for honest DTOs. default(T) zero-inits structs without ctor. Static ctor runs once.
Follow-up: how does SetsRequiredMembers interact with source generators?
commonPitfalls: Saying required means non-null gets you rejected.
Assuming new MyStruct() equals default(MyStruct) when a parameterless constructor exists.
Strong answer: 'required is initialization, not nullability. default(T) skips ctor. Primary ctor capture is not auto-public.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript constructors can return a different object; C# constructors cannot replace `this`. JavaScript has no `required`-property compiler check.
TypeScript definite assignment (`!`) and `required` in types are compile-time only. C# `required` is still compile-time, but `init` accessors are real Intermediate Language (IL).
